articles.title: Record non-DSE admissions to Hong Kong’s universities spark calls for quotas
articles.summary: Hong Kong’s public universities admitted a record number of students applying outside the local Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) exam system, with non-DSE admissions rising by 63 per cent over seven years to nearly 30 per cent of the 15,000 government-funded undergraduate places. Concurrently, DSE student admissions declined by 7 per cent, reducing their share of those places from 82 per cent to 72 per cent.
articles.insight:
Hong Kong’s sharp rise in non-DSE admissions—especially from mainland China—may reflect shifting preferences among high-achieving Chinese students toward alternative pathways, though it’s unclear whether this signals broader regional demand shifts or is specific to Hong Kong’s policy and capacity constraints.  
Admissions teams should monitor mainland Chinese student application trends to their institutions, particularly enrolment patterns of students with international qualifications (e.g., IB, A-levels, AP), and assess whether Hong Kong’s expanded non-DSE intake correlates with changes in outbound mobility intentions or credential recognition policies.

articles.title: Australia: Carolyn Evans warns of fallout from further international student cuts
articles.summary: Carolyn Evans, chair of Universities Australia, warned that universities have become overly reliant on income from international students due to years of public funding cuts. She stressed that any further reduction in international student numbers must be accompanied by a plan to address the resulting financial fallout.
articles.insight:
Australia’s potential international student cuts—driven by fiscal reliance and policy review—may indirectly influence global perceptions of stability and value, though direct demand shifts in other English-speaking destinations remain uncertain without parallel policy changes.  
Admissions teams should monitor Australian visa policy updates, enrolment data trends, and source-market sentiment surveys, particularly among high-intent cohorts in Asia, to assess whether spillover effects emerge in application volumes or destination preferences.

articles.title: US Department of State issued 23% fewer study visas to international students in 2025
articles.summary: The US Department of State issued 23% fewer F-1, M-1, and J-1 student visas to international students in 2025 compared to 2024. Among these, F-1 visa issuances—used by degree-seeking students—declined by one-third during the same period.
articles.insight:
The 23% drop in US student visas—especially the 33% decline in F-1 issuances—may reflect tighter visa adjudication, shifting geopolitical perceptions, or reduced application volumes, though it’s unclear whether this signals weaker underlying demand or procedural constraints.  
Admissions teams should track real-time application and enrolment data by origin country, monitor visa refusal rates and processing times, and assess how peer destinations’ policies and messaging are influencing student decision-making amid evolving global mobility trends.

articles.title: 12-month rolling student visa rejection rate hits 4.9% in the UK
articles.summary: The UK’s 12-month rolling student visa rejection rate reached 4.9% for the period ending June 2026, according to analysis by The PIE of new Home Office data. This figure represents the proportion of student visa applications refused over that 12-month period.
articles.insight:
A modest 4.9% UK student visa refusal rate—within historical norms—suggests no immediate tightening of policy, but rising scrutiny on genuine student intent and financial evidence may subtly shift applicant confidence, particularly among risk-averse markets or lower-income cohorts.  

Admissions teams should track regional refusal trends, especially for high-volume countries, and reinforce pre-application visa readiness support—without overreacting—as Home Office guidance updates or seasonal processing delays could temporarily influence outcomes.

articles.title: Mỹ siết đường thực tập của du học sinh
articles.summary: The United States has implemented a new policy restricting international students from undertaking internships unless their academic program explicitly requires such practical training. This regulation narrows opportunities for foreign students to gain work experience in the U.S. labor market.
articles.insight:
This policy shift may dampen U.S. appeal for Southeast Asian students prioritising post-study work exposure, though its broader impact on enrolment depends on how strictly it’s enforced and whether alternative pathways—like CPT-eligible programmes—remain accessible.  
Admissions teams should track application trends from Southeast Asia, assess the proportion of prospective students citing internship opportunities as a key decision factor, and clarify CPT eligibility early in recruitment communications.
